prompt.context: Our client is a global airline company that wants to introduce wireless Internet services on its international flights (i.e., flights between US cities and non-US cities). While other airline companies already provide wireless services for domestic flights, different technology is required for flights over water because there is no access to wireless towers on land. Currently, there is only one vendor available in the market that provides a new technology allowing wireless Internet over water.
prompt.question: The client wants to know at what price they should deploy this wireless Internet service on international flights.

clarifying_info.q: What is the willingness to pay among passengers?
clarifying_info.a: 30% of passengers are willing to pay if price is under $5/hr; 15% of passengers are willing to pay if price is under $10/hr; 5% of passengers are willing to pay if price is under $20/hr
Investment of $600,000 per airplane for installation and access to wireless technology; $4 per user hour (includes all variable costs)

clarifying_info.q: How many planes and flights are there?
clarifying_info.a: 500 planes flying internationally, 2 flights per day per plane
One international flight can carry 500 passengers; on average flights have 80% capacity, so about 400 passengers

clarifying_info.q: How long are the flights and how long do users spend online?
clarifying_info.a: Average international flight is 8 hours; assume each user spends 3 hours online

framework: Customers: segment passengers by willingness to pay, identify demand at each price point
Profitability: calculate revenue per flight at each candidate price, subtract variable costs, determine contribution margin
Investment payback: divide fixed installation cost per plane by daily profit to find payback period
Recommendation: compare payback periods across pricing options, identify annual profit post-payback, assess risks

questions.prompt: Given the WTP tiers, which price points should the client consider, and why not charge under $5/hr?
questions.guidance: Charging under $5/hr is not profitable because the $4/hr variable cost leaves no margin. The viable candidate prices are $9/hr (targeting 15% of passengers) and $19/hr (targeting 5% of passengers). Charging exactly $5, $10, or $20 is possible but the case uses $9 and $19 as representative prices just below the next WTP threshold.

questions.prompt: Calculate profit per flight at $9/hr and $19/hr.
questions.guidance: At $9/hr: profit margin = $9 - $4 = $5/hr; profit per passenger = $5 * 3 hrs = $15; users per flight = 15% * 400 = 60; profit per flight = $15 * 60 = $900. At $19/hr: profit margin = $19 - $4 = $15/hr; profit per passenger = $15 * 3 hrs = $45; users per flight = 5% * 400 = 20; profit per flight = $45 * 20 = $900. Both prices yield $900/flight.

math.setup: Price options: $9/hr (15% WTP) vs $19/hr (5% WTP). Variable cost = $4/hr. Users per flight = WTP% * 400 passengers. Online time = 3 hrs/user.
math.answer: $900 per flight at either price point

questions.prompt: Calculate the daily profit per plane and the investment payback period.
questions.guidance: Daily profit per plane = $900/flight * 2 flights/day = $1,800/day. Payback period = $600,000 / $1,800 = 333 days, approximately 1 year for both pricing options.

math.setup: Fixed investment = $600,000/plane. Daily profit = profit/flight * 2 flights/day.
math.answer: 333 days (~1 year) for both price options

questions.prompt: What is the annual profit across the entire fleet after the investment is recovered?
questions.guidance: Annual profit = $1,800/day * 365 days * 500 planes = approximately $330 million per year.

math.setup: Fleet = 500 planes, daily profit per plane = $1,800.

brainstorming.prompt: What secondary effects and strategic considerations should the client weigh when deciding whether to launch this service?

categories.name: Revenue upside
ideas: Attracting more passengers who value in-flight connectivity, increasing load factor
Potential to offer tiered pricing (e.g., basic vs. premium bandwidth)

categories.name: Technology and vendor risks
ideas: Single vendor monopoly creates pricing power risk for the vendor
Technology is new and reliability is unproven
Vendor could exit the market or face supply constraints
Maintenance and support complexity over water

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Competitors could adopt the same technology, eliminating differentiation
First-mover advantage in brand perception as the innovator in international connectivity
Risk that competitors negotiate better deals with the same vendor later

categories.name: Operational considerations
ideas: Passenger privacy and security on shared networks
Regulatory approval in different countries for in-flight connectivity

recommendation: The client should deploy wireless Internet on its international flights. The payback period is approximately 1 year regardless of whether the price is set at $9/hr or $19/hr, both yielding $900 profit per flight.

Annual profit across the 500-plane fleet after payback is approximately $330 million. Given the equivalent payback at both prices, the client may prefer $9/hr to drive higher adoption (15% vs. 5%) which could compound through loyalty and brand benefits, or $19/hr to signal premium positioning — further analysis of brand strategy would inform this choice.
risks: Sole vendor dependency creates cost and supply risk; vendor could raise prices or face operational issues
New technology reliability over water is unproven; poor customer experience could damage brand
Competing airlines may adopt the service quickly, eroding first-mover advantage
Regulatory hurdles in international airspace could delay rollout
next_steps: Negotiate a long-term supply contract with the vendor to lock in installation and per-user costs
Run a pilot on a subset of routes to validate WTP assumptions and measure actual usage
Assess competitive timeline to determine urgency of rollout
Evaluate tiered pricing or bundling options to maximize revenue per user
